articles.title: AI robot for seniors can alert family after a call for help
articles.summary: Tuya Smart's Doova AI home robot rolls to seniors who call for help and connects family via live video, but key privacy questions remain unanswered.
articles.body: If you have a parent or grandparent who wants to stay in their own home, you probably know the question that can sit quietly in the back of your mind: What happens if they fall and nobody realizes they need help? Tuya Smart thinks its small artificial intelligence robot could become part of the answer. The company unveiled Doova at IFA 2026 in Berlin. This wheeled AI home companion is designed for seniors who live independently. It can move through the home, respond when someone calls for help and connect family members through live video when an emergency appears to be unfolding. That gets my attention because Doova goes beyond sitting on a table waiting for someone to press a button or call out from across the room. It can actually come to you. And that raises a bigger question: How much could a robot like this really help someone live safely and independently at home? NEW! Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: Get Better Health Care With AI In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will show you five practical ways AI can help you take a more active role in your health care. You’ll learn how to organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare questions for your next doctor’s visit. No technical experience is needed. Register for free now at CyberGuyLive.com THE BEST TIME TO TALK TO YOUR PARENTS ABOUT SENIOR CARE — BEFORE IT'S TOO LATE How Doova responds when a senior calls for help Doova uses LDS LiDAR to navigate around the home. A four-microphone system helps it figure out where a voice is coming from. Meanwhile, AI vision analyzes a person's skeletal posture. If someone falls or needs assistance, they can say, "Hey Tuya, help." Doova then locates the person and rolls over to assess what is happening. Tuya says that if the user does not respond within 60 seconds, Doova starts an emergency response workflow. Family members receive an alert with a two-way live video call so they can see what is happening and arrange assistance. For now, Tuya has not said that Doova automatically detects falls without the user first calling for help or that it directly contacts 911 or a professional monitoring service. So, I would treat it as an added layer of support rather than a replacement for a dedicated medical alert system. Doova wants to be an AI companion too Emergency help is only part of what Tuya has built into Doova. The robot uses a multimodal large language model so people can talk with it in a more natural way instead of memorizing rigid voice commands. For someone spending long stretches at home alone, Doova can carry on a conversation or play entertainment. It can also help make sense of a confusing bill or letter. Another feature caught my eye. Tuya says Doova can identify potential scam risks. YOUR SENIOR PARENTS ARE EASIER TO IMPERSONATE THAN YOU ARE That could be useful for older adults who receive a suspicious message and want a second opinion before responding. However, I would never want someone relying solely on an AI robot to decide whether a bill, email or financial request is legitimate. AI can make mistakes. If Doova flags something suspicious, the safest next move would still be to verify it independently or share it with someone you trust. We've seen how much personal information scammers can gather about older adults, particularly after major life changes such as moving into a retirement community. A WHEELED ROBOT MAY BEAT HUMANOIDS INTO YOUR HOME It can help with everyday routines around the home Doova can remind you to take medication, keep track of your schedule and give you weather updates. Tuya says it can also learn your preferences over time, which could make its suggestions feel more useful day-to-day. The company plans to add a feature that helps find misplaced items around the house. If that works well, I can see the appeal. Plenty of us have spent far too long looking for glasses, keys or a remote that was nearby the whole time. WOULD YOU PAY $8,000 FOR A ROBOT TO FOLD LAUNDRY? Doova can patrol your home while you are away Doova also doubles as a mobile home-monitoring device. Rather than continuously hugging the walls as some patrol robots do, Tuya says Doova travels to selected locations near the center of rooms. From there, it can perform a 360-degree scan. The robot then creates a safety report that can be sent to the user's phone. When the battery runs low, Doova can return to its charging dock on its own. AI CHATBOT PRIVACY: WHAT YOUR AI MAY KNOW ABOUT YOU That gives the robot another possible use when someone travels or spends part of the day away from home. However, this capability also leads straight into the biggest question I have about Doova. What about privacy with Doova? Doova has microphones, AI vision and live video inside the home. It can also learn a user's preferences over time. That can make the robot more helpful, but it also means giving it access to a lot of personal information. We raised similar questions when we looked at another AI home robot that can recognize family members and build personalized memories. With Doova, I would want to know where video and audio are processed, what gets stored, who can see it and whether users can permanently delete what the robot has learned. Tuya's launch announcement does not spell out those Doova-specific privacy controls. Until it does, that is something I would look closely at before bringing a camera-equipped AI robot into a loved one's home. You can also review our guide to limiting the information popular AI services collect about you. Doova can control your smart home Tuya also designed Doova to work as a central smart home controller. A senior could use voice commands to adjust connected lights or curtains. Doova can also interact with compatible kitchen and bathroom devices. I like the thinking here. Smart homes can become complicated very quickly, especially when every device has its own app. If Doova can put those controls into a simple conversation, that could make smart home technology far easier to use. The robot has a 10.1-inch HD display with animated facial expressions. Its rounded design also looks more like a friendly household companion than an industrial machine. What we still do not know about Doova There are still some important blanks to fill in. Tuya has not announced a retail price or when consumers will actually be able to buy Doova. I also want to see how it handles a real home. Rugs, cords and tight spaces can trip up mobile robots. Stairs are another obvious challenge for something that moves around on wheels. The bigger question is how dependable Doova would be during an actual emergency. Someone may be frightened, speaking softly or lying somewhere the robot cannot easily reach. That is where real-world testing will tell us much more than a demonstration on the show floor. We reached out to Tuya Smart with questions about Doova's emergency response, privacy protections, connectivity and availability, but did not hear back before our deadline. What this means to you If you are helping a parent or loved one age in place, Doova gives us a pretty good look at where home technology is heading. Instead of relying only on stationary smart speakers or cameras, future AI assistants may move around the house and respond to what is happening nearby. That could give families another way to stay connected while allowing older adults to maintain more independence. However, I would look closely at the emergency process before relying on any product like this. Find out who gets contacted and what happens when the internet fails. You should also understand exactly what the cameras and microphones collect. Finally, think about the person who will actually use it. The best technology in the world offers little value if someone finds it confusing, intrusive or uncomfortable. Kurt's key takeaways What interests me most about Doova is the move from passive smart devices toward AI that can physically come to you. For an older adult who wants to remain independent, having a robot respond to a call for help and bring family into the situation quickly could offer real peace of mind. Still, I would want much more information before trusting Doova with someone I love. Safety technology has to prove itself outside the controlled environment of a trade show. I want to know how reliably it reaches someone during an emergency and how much personal information it collects along the way. The privacy side deserves just as much attention. A moving camera and microphone that learns your routines can become incredibly helpful. It can also become one of the most intimate connected devices in your home. Doova has an interesting idea at its core. Now Tuya needs to show that the technology can earn the level of trust its role requires. Would you put an AI robot with cameras and microphones in an aging parent's home if it could help family respond faster during an emergency, or would that feel like too much surveillance? articles.body: Between differing diet plans, food intolerances and conflicting work schedules, some couples are choosing "food divorce" — a term circulating on social media for partners who intentionally cook, order and eat their meals separately. While taking separate paths at mealtime might solve logistical headaches, experts warn that splitting up at the dinner table can come at a cost to the relationship. Shared family meals can help people reconnect, build stronger emotional bonds and reduce stress, according to health institutions like Mayo Clinic. ‘QUIET QUITTING’ IN MARRIAGE: THE SUBTLE SIGNS A SPOUSE HAS EMOTIONALLY CHECKED OUT For couples, experts say regularly eating apart could become a concern if it reflects broader emotional distance or reduces opportunities to spend meaningful time together. Nutrition experts emphasize the issue is often less about the food itself and more about the lost opportunity for a built-in daily checkpoint. "I think it reflects many people's very busy schedules," Tanya Freirich, a North Carolina-based registered dietitian nutritionist, told Fox News Digital. "Mealtime can be a time to unite, to communicate, to build social relationships and foster a connection," she said. "If we're eating completely alone or at different times than important people in our lives, it may foster a little bit of disconnection." DOCTORS SAY 8 FORGOTTEN HABITS COULD HELP FIGHT STRESS, OBESITY AND CHRONIC DISEASE Eating separately can contribute to a "roommate dynamic," experts note. Without regular time to reconnect and discuss the day, couples may have fewer opportunities for communication. The practice can also contribute to isolation, according to Freirich. "If so many Americans are eating every meal alone for many days or most of their days, that certainly can't be great for mental health or well-being." There can also be practical drawbacks, as preparing separate meals or ordering from different restaurants may increase grocery costs, preparation time and kitchen cleanup. Studies show people dining alone are more likely to eat quickly, mindlessly scroll on their phones, or settle for heavily processed convenience foods compared to when they share meals with others. "Communities all around the world for thousands of years have come together around mealtimes." Couples can accommodate different dietary needs without preparing entirely separate meals. For those navigating specific calorie targets, plant-based diets or medical restrictions, Freirich recommended building "modular" or "choose your own adventure" meals as a more efficient method. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES "Something like a deconstructed taco night, grain bowls, a pasta or noodle night, or even a sheet pan meal where you're creating each food on its own," the expert said. "So the protein, the carb, the veggies are being cooked separately. And then you get to decide your portions and make your own meal from those ingredients that can meet everyone's needs." When conflicting schedules or caregiving duties make daily dinners impossible, experts recommend prioritizing quality over frequency. Even sharing a quick weekend breakfast or setting aside one designated night a week can help maintain connection. Put the phone away and actually enjoy the other person's company."

articles.title: Why are Americans so tired? CDC report highlights who is feeling it most
articles.summary: About 71% of of adults in the U.S. say they experience fatigue, a new report from the CDC found. Women and younger adults are feeling it most often.
articles.body:
The cost of healthcare . Economic uncertainties . Fears of AI-associated end times . It's enough to exhaust anyone.

About 71.5% of adults in the United States say they experienced fatigue on multiple days over the past three months, according to a new report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS). Women and younger adults are more likely to report frequent fatigue, meaning most days or every day, than men are.

Sociologist Natalie A.E. Young, lead author of the report, said fatigue is "one of the most frequently reported health concerns in primary care visits in the U.S." It's the first study about general fatigue from NCHS, which surveyed about 27,000 adults ages 18 and older in 2024 about their health and daily lives.

People with fatigue "are at higher risk of activity limitations and disability, including permanent work disability. Yet there hadn't been much attention to the frequency of general fatigue symptoms in the U.S. adult population," Young said.

Fatigue isn't ordinary sleepiness . It's "physical or mental tiredness or exhaustion that does not improve with additional sleep or rest," the researchers said. General fatigue, which is different from chronic fatigue syndrome , can be a symptom of other health problems or a side effect of medication.

Fatigue is often connected to other health problems, difficulty concentrating and limited social activities. People with symptoms of frequent fatigue were more likely to experience "co-occurring functioning difficulties," including cognitive difficulties, depression and anxiety, said Young.

"So it's not just that fatigue is common," she said. "It's that fatigue is common and those with fatigue are facing limitations in their daily lives."

Adults who experienced frequent fatigue were more than three times as likely to have symptoms of depression and about twice as likely to report cognitive difficulties or symptoms of anxiety, compared to those who don't experience it, the study found.

Nearly 3 in 4 adults felt "very tired or exhausted" at least some days in the past three months.

About 1 in 6 adults experienced frequent fatigue, defined as feeling very tired or exhausted "most days" or "every day."

Frequent fatigue was highest among younger adults, ages 18-34 years (19.5%), with the lowest rate among adults ages 65 and older (12.9%).

Women were more likely than men to report frequent fatigue (20% versus 13%).

American Indian and Alaska Native adults had the highest rate of frequent fatigue (25.5%), followed by white adults (18%), Black adults (17.3%) and Hispanic adults (12.9%), with Asian adults having the lowest rate of frequent fatigue (9.1%).

Adults living in the South (17.7%) and Midwest (17.5%) were more likely to experience frequent fatigue than adults living in the West (15.6%) or Northeast (14.5%), the report showed.

The CDC survey didn't look at underlying causes of frequent fatigue and it doesn't indicate whether it's worse than in previous years.

But Dr. Alana A. Lewis, a cardiologist at the Bluhm Cardiovascular Institute at Northwestern Medicine in Chicago, said the findings were "not unexpected."

"Just living in this country, we all, at some point, feel fatigue," Lewis said.

In the most recent "Stress in America " survey, the American Psychological Association found that a majority of adults reported feeling isolated, left out and more stressed about the future than they used to be.

Stress can cause surges in hormones like cortisol and adrenaline, which can wear a body down. That increasing stress contributes to an uptick in fatigue, said Jennifer Caspari, a clinical psychologist licensed in Denver and Vancouver, British Columbia.

"People are incredibly busy," Caspari said. "They're stressed. They're feeling spread thin. They have a lot on their plates and only so many hours in the day. They're trying to cram in so much."

Stress can also lead to mental health issues like anxiety and depression, which can disrupt sleep, causing us to feel more tired throughout the day, Caspari said.

More than half of women said they felt fatigue "some days," and 20% experienced it "most days or every day."

Caspari said chronic health issues, like autoimmune diseases, which often include fatigue as a symptom, affect women in greater numbers. Hormonal fluctuations during menstruation, pregnancy, perimenopause and menopause can also affect energy levels.

And many women in heterosexual relationships, for example, say they feel they have more responsibilities at work and home than their male partners do, which can lead to them feeling exhausted, Caspari said.

Even when tasks are evenly divided, women experience stress differently. They tend to worry more about organizing and planning and engage in more "internal dialogue" about their responsibilities.

Mental health, lifestyle and physical health are the "three big pillars" that can trigger fatigue, Lewis said. Heart disease, obstructive sleep apnea, anemia and thyroid issues can also be underlying causes of fatigue.

When patients complain of fatigue, Lewis asks:

"Start with the basics," said Lewis, who encourages patients to follow the American Heart Association's Life's Essential 8 cardiovascular health checklist.

Pay attention to your sleep and stress patterns to determine whether fatigue is a temporary issue or something that's become more "chronic and persistent," which could indicate a medical problem.

Learning to relax, both physically and mentally, is important, said Caspari. Take a break from never-ending to-do lists. "You're not a robot. You only have so much energy," Caspari said.

Passive resting, like sitting down to watch TV, is perfectly fine. Caspari also recommends "active rest," low-intensity activities like breathing exercises and gentle stretching.

"Active rest can feel more nourishing," she said, "and it can have a more helpful impact on the fatigue over time rather than just sitting and scrolling."

articles.title: Omagh: Man charged following armed bus hijacking
articles.summary: The charges include kidnapping, hijacking, aggravated vehicle taking causing injury and possession of an offensive weapon.
articles.body:
A 39-year-old man has been charged with a number of offences after a bus was hijacked in County Tyrone on Saturday .

The driver of the bus was threatened at knife point by a man, who then allowed passengers to leave the bus. However, the bus driver was kept on board.

The charges include kidnapping, hijacking, aggravated vehicle taking causing injury and possession of an offensive weapon.

The man will appear before Enniskillen Magistrates Court on Monday.

Videos circulating on social media appeared to show a Translink Goldliner coach being driven at speed through residential streets while being chased by a Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) patrol car.

Police said the bus was hijacked in the Beltany Road area of Omagh, Co Tyrone, shortly before 13:00 BST on Saturday.

The man who hijacked the bus then made off in the direction of Newtownstewart and a pursuit ensued along the A5 through Victoria Bridge and Sion Mills. The pursuit lasted nearly 20 miles.

"The bus was eventually stopped in the Head of the Town area of Strabane and a man, aged in his 30s was removed from the bus and subsequently arrested," said a PSNI spokesperson.

The Northern Ireland Ambulance Service (NIAS) said two people were taken to South West Acute Hospital for treatment.

articles.title: Popular GLP-1 weight-loss drugs linked to potentially deadly brain disorder
articles.summary: A study linked 15 cases of Wernicke encephalopathy to GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic and Mounjaro, raising concerns about vitamin B1 deficiency risks.
articles.body: Researchers are warning about a rare but potentially life-threatening brain condition that may be linked to popular GLP-1 weight-loss medications. A new study, published in Clinical Nutrition, identified 15 reported cases of Wernicke encephalopathy, a neurological disorder caused by severe vitamin B1 deficiency, in people taking GLP-1 receptor agonists. Most of the reported cases involved semaglutide, sold under the brand names Ozempic and Wegovy, or tirzepatide, sold as Mounjaro and Zepbound. DOCTORS REVEAL HIDDEN DANGER FOR SOME OZEMPIC, WEGOVY USERS WITH BRAIN DISORDERS Researchers found 15 cases through the FDA's Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS), published medical literature and their own medical center. Most patients reported gastrointestinal symptoms or nutritional issues, including weight loss, vomiting, loss of appetite or malnutrition, the study noted. Reports of the disorder appeared more often among people taking GLP-1 medications than among those taking other drugs, the researchers found. They emphasized, however, that the study cannot prove the medications caused the condition. Vitamin B1 plays an important role in brain function, the researchers said. Severe deficiencies can cause confusion, trouble walking, balance problems and vision changes. If left untreated, the condition can lead to permanent neurological damage or death. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Karthik Achari, a Chicago-based clinician and founder of PepMD who was not involved in the study, said the findings should be viewed in perspective. "Researchers went through adverse event reports and the medical literature and found a small number of cases, 15, of Wernicke encephalopathy in people taking GLP-1 drugs," Achari told Fox News Digital. "That's out of millions of people on these medications. So this is rare." "But it's real, it's serious, and the mechanism makes sense," he added. GLP-1 medications can reduce appetite while also causing nausea and vomiting, making it easier for some people to become deficient in vitamin B1, Achari said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "The drug shrinks your appetite. It doesn't shrink your body's requirements," he said. "You can now eat very little without feeling it, which is the point of the medication, but your need for protein, vitamins, and fluids didn't go anywhere." People with persistent nausea and vomiting, those losing weight very quickly while eating little, people with a history of bariatric surgery and those who use alcohol heavily may face a higher risk, Achari said. Erin Palinski-Wade, a New Jersey-based nutritionist and author of "The Sleepdemic Solution," said proper nutrition and hydration should be considered part of treatment while taking GLP-1 medications. "GLP-1 medications can dramatically reduce appetite, but that also means people may unintentionally under-eat the very things their bodies need most, especially protein, fiber and fluids," she told Fox News Digital. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Palinski-Wade said ongoing vomiting or diarrhea can increase the risk of dehydration and kidney problems. She urged patients to seek medical guidance if those symptoms continue for roughly 24 hours. "Don't assume every side effect is just part of being on a GLP-1," Palinski-Wade said. "Severe or persistent symptoms deserve attention." The researchers acknowledged that the study relied largely on reports submitted to the FDA and cannot prove GLP-1 medications caused the condition. They called for additional research, and experts said patients should not stop taking prescribed GLP-1 medications based on these findings alone. articles.title: Pennsylvania woman dies from measles complications, state’s third death this year
articles.summary: A 40-year-old woman has died from measles complications in Pennsylvania, marking the state’s third measles-associated death this year as the U.S. experiences its worst resurgence of the highly contagious disease in 35 years.
articles.body: A 40-year-old woman has died from measles complications in Pennsylvania, marking the state’s third measles-associated death this year as the U.S. experiences its worst resurgence of the highly contagious disease in 35 years. The woman, a Jefferson County resident, died on Saturday, county Coroner Greg Furlong said on Facebook. “This is a heartbreaking loss for the family and an unfortunate reminder that measles can be a serious and potentially life-threatening disease,” Furlong said. No other information about the woman will be released, he added. The Pennsylvania Department of Health said it was aware of the death reported by the Jefferson County coroner. “The Department of Health is conducting a thorough review of this case and will provide the public with updated information when it becomes available,” health officials said in a statement. At least 676 measles cases have been confirmed in 37 counties in Pennsylvania so far this year, the state’s health officials reported Friday. The outbreak has hospitalized 124 people in the state. Of the confirmed cases, fewer than 1% had been fully vaccinated, Pennsylvania health officials said. The woman is the third person reported to have died in connection with measles in Pennsylvania. The two other measles-related deaths involved infants, according to the Lancaster County coroner, Dr. Stephen Diamantoni. Measles symptoms typically begin with a cough, fever, runny nose and red, watery eyes, followed by a red rash. The disease can cause severe complications, including pneumonia and swelling of the brain. The Jefferson County coroner’s office is working with Pennsylvania health officials on the case, Furlong posted. The U.S. is experiencing its largest measles outbreak since 1991, with more than 3,000 confirmed cases this year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
